claim: Millions of neurons drive the activity of hundreds of muscles, meaning many different neural population activity patterns could generate the same movement.
source: Millions of neurons drive the activity of hundreds of muscles, meaning many different neural population activity patterns could generate the same movement.
evidence: This is a general statement about neural redundancy in motor control, drawing from established understanding of the motor system.

claim: Redundant (i.e. behaviorally equivalent) activity patterns may be beneficial for neural computation.
source: Studies have suggested that these redundant (i.e. behaviorally equivalent) activity patterns may be beneficial for neural computation.
evidence: This claim references previous studies suggesting computational benefits of redundancy.

claim: The distributions of redundant neural activity and task-relevant activity were coupled.
source: Surprisingly, the distributions of redundant neural activity and task-relevant activity were coupled, which enabled accurate predictions of the distributions of redundant activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Principles inspired by work on muscular redundancy did not accurately predict the distributions of redundant neural activity.
source: Principles inspired by work on muscular redundancy did not accurately predict these distributions.
evidence: This is a primary finding from comparing predictions to observed data.

claim: Neural redundancy may allow us to prepare movements without executing them.
source: For example, neural redundancy may allow us to prepare movements without executing them (Kaufman et al., 2014; Elsayed et al., 2016), enable stable computation despite unstable neural dynamics (Driscoll et al., 2017; Druckmann and Chklovskii, 2012; Murray et al., 2017) and allow the central nervous system to filter out unwanted noise (Moreno-Bote et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Neural redundancy may enable stable computation despite unstable neural dynamics.
source: For example, neural redundancy may allow us to prepare movements without executing them (Kaufman et al., 2014; Elsayed et al., 2016), enable stable computation despite unstable neural dynamics (Driscoll et al., 2017; Druckmann and Chklovskii, 2012; Murray et al., 2017) and allow the central nervous system to filter out unwanted noise (Moreno-Bote et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Neural redundancy may allow the central nervous system to filter out unwanted noise.
source: For example, neural redundancy may allow us to prepare movements without executing them (Kaufman et al., 2014; Elsayed et al., 2016), enable stable computation despite unstable neural dynamics (Driscoll et al., 2017; Druckmann and Chklovskii, 2012; Murray et al., 2017) and allow the central nervous system to filter out unwanted noise (Moreno-Bote et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: If two population activity patterns are read out equivalently, the brain should prefer the pattern that requires less energy to produce.
source: However, a commonly held assumption is that neural activity might also be constrained by energetics: All things being equal, if two population activity patterns are read out equivalently, the brain should prefer the pattern that requires less energy to produce (Laughlin et al., 1998; Barlow, 1969; Levy and Baxter, 1996).
evidence: This claim is presented as a commonly held assumption supported by citations.

claim: During arm movements, different combinations of muscle activity can lead to the same arm kinematics.
source: During arm movements, different combinations of muscle activity can lead to the same arm kinematics, meaning these different muscle activity patterns are redundant.
evidence: This is a well-established principle in motor control.

claim: Muscle activity should require minimum energy relative to other redundant options.
source: First, because muscle contraction requires energy in the form of ATP, the selected muscle activity should require minimum energy relative to the other redundant options (Thoroughman and Shadmehr, 1999; Huang et al., 2012; Fagg et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work on muscle redundancy.

claim: A minimal intervention strategy has been proposed in which subjects control only the aspects of muscle activity that influence the task outcome.
source: Second, a minimal intervention strategy has been proposed in which subjects control only the aspects of muscle activity that influence the task outcome, and allow for variability in the aspects of muscle activity that do not influence the task outcome (Scholz and Schöner, 1999; Todorov and Jordan, 2002; Valero-Cuevas et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The activity of around thirty muscles in the arm and hand is controlled by tens of thousands of neurons in the spinal cord.
source: During arm movements, the activity of around thirty muscles in the arm and hand is controlled by tens of thousands of neurons in the spinal cord (Gray, 1918; Feinstein et al., 1955).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: Spinal cord neurons are influenced by millions of neurons in the primary motor cortex and other motor areas.
source: Those neurons are in turn influenced by millions of neurons in the primary motor cortex and other motor areas (Ettema et al., 1998; Lemon, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to neuroanatomical studies.

claim: The neural control of arm movement is redundant.
source: Thus, the neural control of arm movement is redundant (Figure 1A), in that different population activity patterns can generate the same movement (Rokni et al., 2007; Ajemian et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Three Rhesus macaques were trained to perform a brain-computer interface task in which they controlled the velocity of a cursor by modulating neural activity in primary motor cortex.
source: We trained three Rhesus macaques to perform a brain-computer interface task in which they controlled the velocity of a cursor on a computer screen by volitionally modulating neural activity in primary motor cortex.
evidence: This describes the experimental setup used in the study.

claim: The distribution of redundant activity may be coupled with the task-relevant activity, so that producing particular activity patterns in output-potent dimensions requires changing the distribution of activity in output-null dimensions.
source: Third, we considered the possibility that the distribution of redundant activity may be coupled with the task-relevant activity, so that producing particular activity patterns in output-potent dimensions requires changing the distribution of activity in output-null dimensions.
evidence: This is one of the hypotheses tested in the study.

claim: The results of Sadtler et al. (2014) indicate that neural activity cannot readily leave the intrinsic manifold.
source: The results of Sadtler et al. (2014) indicate that neural activity cannot readily leave this manifold, and more recent results demonstrate that neural activity is further constrained by a neural repertoire within the intrinsic manifold (Golub et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim references findings from previous studies.

claim: Neural activity is constrained by a neural repertoire within the intrinsic manifold.
source: The results of Sadtler et al. (2014) indicate that neural activity cannot readily leave this manifold, and more recent results demonstrate that neural activity is further constrained by a neural repertoire within the intrinsic manifold (Golub et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim references findings from a previous study.

claim: There is strong evidence that redundant activity is coupled with task-relevant activity.
source: We found strong evidence for the third hypothesis, that redundant activity is coupled with task-relevant activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claim: Neural redundancy is resolved differently than muscular redundancy.
source: This indicates that neural redundancy is resolved differently than muscular redundancy.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The output-null space should not be thought of as a space in which neural activity can freely vary to carry out computations without regard to the output-potent activity.
source: Furthermore, the output-null space should not be thought of as a space in which neural activity can freely vary to carry out computations without regard to the output-potent activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The distribution of output-null activity is constrained by the corresponding output-potent activity.
source: Instead, the distribution of output-null activity is constrained by the corresponding output-potent activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claim: 85–94 neural units were recorded using a Utah array in the primary motor cortex in each of three Rhesus macaques.
source: To study the selection of redundant neural activity, we used a BCI based on 85–94 neural units recorded using a Utah array in the primary motor cortex in each of three Rhesus macaques.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods and data collection.

claim: Animals modulated their neural activity to move a computer cursor in a 2D center-out task.
source: Animals modulated their neural activity to move a computer cursor in a 2D center-out task (see Materials and methods; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental task.

claim: A two-dimensional subspace of the 10-dimensional intrinsic manifold was mapped to horizontal and vertical cursor velocity and was therefore output-potent.
source: A two-dimensional subspace of the 10-dimensional intrinsic manifold was mapped to horizontal and vertical cursor velocity and was therefore output-potent, while the eight orthogonal dimensions were output-null.
evidence: This describes the experimental design and BCI mapping.

claim: Eight orthogonal dimensions were output-null.
source: A two-dimensional subspace of the 10-dimensional intrinsic manifold was mapped to horizontal and vertical cursor velocity and was therefore output-potent, while the eight orthogonal dimensions were output-null.
evidence: This describes the experimental design and BCI mapping.

claim: The Minimal Firing hypothesis predicted that subjects would select the population activity pattern requiring the fewest spikes among all patterns that produce the same cursor movement.
source: Because spiking incurs a metabolic cost (Laughlin, 2001; Laughlin et al., 1998), we first considered the hypothesis that among all the population activity patterns that produce the same cursor movement, the subject will select the one requiring the fewest spikes (Barlow, 1969; Softky and Kammen, 1991; Levy and Baxter, 1996).
evidence: This describes one of the hypotheses tested, supported by citations.

claim: The Minimal Deviation hypothesis yielded an average histogram error of 30.9% ±1.2% (mean ± SE) across sessions.
source: This hypothesis yielded an average histogram error of 30.9% ±1.2% (mean ± SE) across sessions.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from comparing predictions to observed data.

claim: Muscle activity exhibits more variability in output-null dimensions than in output-potent dimensions.
source: It has been shown that muscle activity exhibits more variability in output-null dimensions than in output-potent dimensions (Scholz and Schöner, 1999; Todorov and Jordan, 2002; Valero-Cuevas et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work on muscle control.

claim: The predictions of the Uncontrolled-uniform hypothesis differed from the observed output-null activity by 56.6% ±1.1% (mean ± SE) across sessions.
source: The predictions of the Uncontrolled-uniform hypothesis differed from the observed output-null activity by 56.6% ±1.1% (mean ± SE) across sessions.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from comparing predictions to observed data.

claim: The Uncontrolled-empirical hypothesis predictions differed from the observed data by only 23.8% ±0.8% (mean ± SE) across sessions.
source: The histograms of the predictions differed from the observed data by only 23.8% ±0.8% (mean ± SE) across sessions, which is the lowest error of all hypotheses considered so far.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from comparing predictions to observed data.

claim: Previously observed population activity offers greater predictive power of the selection of output-null activity than a priori predictions.
source: This suggests that previously observed population activity (in this case, recorded during use of a different BCI mapping) offers greater predictive power of the selection of output-null activity than a priori predictions such as those of the Minimal Firing, Minimal Deviation, and Uncontrolled-uniform hypotheses.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the prediction errors of different hypotheses.

claim: The predictions of the Persistent Strategy hypothesis differed from the observed output-null activity by 17.4% ±0.7% (mean ± SE) across sessions.
source: The predictions of this hypothesis (Figure 4B–C) differed from the observed output-null activity by 17.4% ±0.7% (mean ± SE) across sessions.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from comparing predictions to observed data.

claim: The dimensions of the intrinsic manifold persist even under different BCI mappings.
source: Previous work has found that the characteristic ways in which neurons covary (i.e. the dimensions of the intrinsic manifold) persist even under different BCI mappings, perhaps owing to underlying network constraints (Sadtler et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim references findings from a previous study.

claim: The predictions of the Fixed Distribution hypothesis differed from the observed output-null activity by only 13.4% ±0.5% (mean ± SE) across sessions.
source: Overall, these predictions differed from the observed output-null activity by only 13.4% ±0.5% (mean ± SE) across sessions.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from comparing predictions to observed data.

claim: The Fixed Distribution hypothesis yielded a lower histogram error than all other hypotheses across sessions from three different animals.
source: The Fixed Distribution hypothesis yielded a lower histogram error than all other hypotheses across sessions from three different animals (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from comparing all hypotheses across experimental data.

claim: The Fixed Distribution hypothesis had the lowest histogram error in 41 of 42 sessions.
source: In total, the Fixed Distribution hypothesis had the lowest histogram error in 41 of 42 sessions.
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of the experimental results.

claim: The mean and covariance of output-null activity was best predicted by the Fixed Distribution hypothesis, with an average mean error of 23.5 ± 1.4 spikes/s (mean ± SE) and an average covariance error of 1.4 ± 0.1 (mean ± SE).
source: In agreement with our findings for histogram error, the mean (Figure 5B) and covariance (Figure 5C) of output-null activity was best predicted by the Fixed Distribution hypothesis, with an average mean error of 23.5 ± 1.4 spikes/s (mean ± SE) and an average covariance error of 1.4 ± 0.1 (mean ± SE in arbitrary units; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from comparing predictions to observed data.

claim: The errors of Fixed Distribution were exceedingly close to the lowest achievable error given the number of samples available.
source: The errors of Fixed Distribution were exceedingly close to the lowest achievable error given the number of samples available (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a comparison of the Fixed Distribution hypothesis performance to an estimated error floor.

claim: The variance of population activity did not change dramatically in dimensions that were output-potent under the first mapping and output-null under the second mapping.
source: These analyses show that, contrary to the predictions of the minimal firing and uncontrolled hypotheses, the variance of population activity did not change dramatically in dimensions that were output-potent under the first mapping and output-null under the second mapping.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data analysis.

claim: If the activity in output-null dimensions is constrained by the output-potent activity, then this may limit the ability of output-null activity to perform computations without affecting the readout.
source: However, if the activity in output-null dimensions is constrained by the output-potent activity, then this may limit the ability of output-null activity to perform computations without affecting the readout.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the experimental findings.

claim: The way in which neural redundancy is resolved is different from how muscle redundancy is resolved.
source: Our results indicate that the way in which neural redundancy is resolved is different from how muscle redundancy is resolved.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the experimental findings to previous work on muscle redundancy.

claim: Models incorporating minimal energy principles have helped to explain observed gait and arm reaches.
source: Models incorporating minimal energy principles have helped to explain observed gait (McNeill Alexander and McNeill, 2002) and arm reaches (Thoroughman and Shadmehr, 1999; Huang et al., 2012; Fagg et al., 2002; Farshchiansadegh et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Minimal energy principles in terms of firing rates do not play a dominant role in the selection of output-null neural activity.
source: However, we found that minimal energy principles in terms of firing rates do not play a dominant role in the selection of output-null neural activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: OFC models have been widely used to explain muscle activity during motor tasks.
source: OFC models have been widely used to explain muscle activity during motor tasks (Todorov, 2004; Scott, 2004; Diedrichsen et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: OFC implementations predict that variability in task-irrelevant dimensions should be higher than variability in task-relevant dimensions.
source: First, those implementations of OFC predict that variability in task-irrelevant dimensions should be higher than variability in task-relevant dimensions, a concept often referred to as the 'uncontrolled manifold' (Scholz and Schöner, 1999).
evidence: This claim describes predictions from OFC models, supported by citations.

claim: The variability of neural activity did not increase in dimensions that went from being task-relevant to task-irrelevant.
source: We found that the variability of neural activity did not increase in dimensions that went from being task-relevant to task-irrelevant (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: OFC implementations predict a 'minimal intervention' strategy, whereby activity in task-relevant dimensions is corrected independently of activity in task-irrelevant dimensions.
source: Second, those implementations of OFC predict a 'minimal intervention' strategy, whereby activity in task-relevant dimensions is corrected independently of activity in task-irrelevant dimensions (Todorov and Jordan, 2002; Valero-Cuevas et al., 2009; Diedrichsen et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim describes predictions from OFC models, supported by citations.

claim: None of the hypotheses incorporating the minimal intervention principle predicted neural activity in task-irrelevant dimensions as accurately as did the Fixed Distribution hypothesis.
source: None of these hypotheses predicted neural activity in task-irrelevant dimensions as accurately as did the Fixed Distribution hypothesis, which predicts that the distributions of task-relevant and task-irrelevant activity are yoked.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the prediction errors of different hypotheses.

claim: It has been proposed that muscle recruitment is habitual rather than optimal, such that muscle recruitment under altered dynamics is a rescaled version of that under normal control.
source: It has also been proposed that muscle recruitment is habitual rather than optimal, such that muscle recruitment under altered dynamics is a rescaled version of that under normal control (de Rugy et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Subjects appear to use the same distribution of activity in each of two different BCI mappings.
source: However, the results for habitual control are different from our findings in that we found that subjects appear to use the same distribution of activity in each of two different BCI mappings, whereas different (overlapping) subsets of muscle activation patterns were used under different conditions in de Rugy et al. (2012).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data, contrasted with previous work.

claim: Conditioning on only the two output-potent dimensions could provide substantial explanatory power for predicting the distribution in the remaining neural dimensions.
source: Given how many dimensions of population activity there are (in this case, 10), it is somewhat surprising that conditioning on only the two output-potent dimensions could provide so much explanatory power for predicting the distribution in the remaining neural dimensions.
evidence: This is an observation about the experimental findings.

claim: Many of the dimensions of population activity are coupled, that is, changing the activity along some dimensions may also lead to changes along other dimensions.
source: This suggests that many of the dimensions of population activity are coupled, that is, changing the activity along some dimensions may also lead to changes along other dimensions, even though those dimensions are mutually orthogonal.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The present work goes beyond Golub et al. (2018) by seeking to determine the constraints on activity in the task-irrelevant (i.e. output-null) dimensions.
source: Although the two studies analyzed data from the same experiments, they ask distinct questions. Golub et al. (2018) focused on explaining the changes in population activity underlying behavioral learning. By contrast, in the present work we seek to determine the constraints on activity in the task-irrelevant (i.e. output-null) dimensions.
evidence: This describes the relationship between the current study and previous work.

claim: Golub et al. (2018) found that the amount of learning animals showed was consistent with a fixed neural repertoire of population activity patterns being reassociated to control the second BCI mapping.
source: Golub et al. (2018) found that the amount of learning animals showed was consistent with a fixed neural repertoire of population activity patterns being reassociated to control the second BCI mapping.
evidence: This claim references findings from a previous study.

claim: The present results represent a stronger constraint on population activity than that shown in Golub et al. (2018).
source: Because many different distributions of neural activity can be constructed from a fixed repertoire, the present results represent a stronger constraint on population activity than that shown in Golub et al. (2018).
evidence: This is a comparison of the current findings to previous work.

claim: The animal's arm was not moving during BCI control.
source: However, in these experiments, the animal's arm was not moving during BCI control (see Extended Data Figure 5 in Sadtler et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental conditions, supported by a citation.

claim: The activity studied here resides within the arm's output-null dimensions.
source: Thus, the activity we study here resides within the arm's output-null dimensions.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the experimental conditions.

claim: Arm movements (or the lack thereof) are unlikely to explain the coupling observed between the output-potent and output-null dimensions of the BCI.
source: This implies that in our recordings the arm's output-potent dimensions do not overlap with either the output-potent or the output-null dimensions of the BCI, and so arm movements (or the lack thereof) are unlikely to explain the coupling we observed between the output-potent and output-null dimensions of the BCI.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the experimental conditions and findings.

claim: The authors were able to accurately predict the output-null distributions (13% histogram error on average, with the lowest possible error being 7%).
source: The fact that we were able to accurately predict the output-null distributions (13% histogram error on average, with the lowest possible error being 7%) without knowing all the potent dimensions is then evidence that these extra potent dimensions, if they exist, would not provide substantial additional predictive power.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data analysis.

claim: The authors used a balanced center-out task design in which subjects made roughly equal numbers of movements in each direction.
source: First, we used a balanced center-out task design in which subjects made roughly equal numbers of movements in each direction.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: This study focused on short timescales, where output-null activity was predicted within one to two hours of subjects learning a new BCI mapping.
source: Second, this study focused on short timescales, where we predicted output-null activity within one to two hours of subjects learning a new BCI mapping.
evidence: This describes the temporal scope of the study.

claim: The best hypothesis (Fixed Distribution) yielded predictions of the distributions of output-null activity whose marginal histograms differed from the data by only 13% on average.
source: Although the hypotheses we tested are not exhaustive, the best hypothesis (Fixed Distribution) yielded predictions of the distributions of output-null activity whose marginal histograms differed from the data by only 13% on average (Figure 4F), where we estimated the lowest error possible to be 7% on average.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from comparing predictions to observed data.

claim: The central premise of the null space concept is that some aspects of neural activity are read out by downstream areas (output-potent) while other aspects are not (output-null).
source: The central premise of the null space concept is that some aspects of neural activity are read out by downstream areas (output-potent) while other aspects are not (output-null) (Kaufman et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes a key concept in the field, supported by a citation.

claim: Activity fluctuations that lie outside of a stimulus encoding space (i.e. 'stimulus-null') are not detrimental to the stimulus information encoded by the neurons.
source: This idea is related to the study of noise correlations, where it was recognized that activity fluctuations that lie outside of a stimulus encoding space (i.e. 'stimulus-null') are not detrimental to the stimulus information encoded by the neurons (Averbeck et al., 2006; Moreno-Bote et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Structuring neural activity in an appropriate null space can allow for multiplexing of different types of information.
source: Studies have also shown that structuring neural activity in an appropriate null space can allow for multiplexing of different types of information (Mante et al., 2013; Raposo et al., 2014), as well as stable behavior (Leonardo, 2005; Rokni et al., 2007; Ajemian et al., 2013) and stable working memory (Druckmann and Chklovskii, 2012; Murray et al., 2017) in the presence of time-varying neural activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The existence of output-null dimensions in the motor system may facilitate motor learning.
source: Additionally, the existence of output-null dimensions in the motor system may facilitate motor learning (Moorman et al., 2017; Ranganathan et al., 2013; Singh et al., 2016) or allow for motor preparation (Kaufman et al., 2014; Elsayed et al., 2016) or novel feedback processing (Stavisky et al., 2017) without causing overt movement.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: There may be limits on the extent to which output-null activity might be leveraged for neural computation.
source: Our work suggests that there may be limits on the extent to which output-null activity might be leveraged for neural computation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The coupling between the distributions of output-null and output-potent activity suggests that output-null activity is not modified independently of output-potent activity.
source: The coupling we observe between the distributions of output-null and output-potent activity suggests that output-null activity is not modified independently of output-potent activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: This coupling may cause activity fluctuations in a stimulus-null space to influence the downstream readout, or limit one's ability to plan the next movement without influencing the current movement.
source: This coupling may cause activity fluctuations in a stimulus-null space to influence the downstream readout, or limit one's ability to plan the next movement without influencing the current movement.
evidence: This is a speculation about the implications of the experimental findings.

claim: 85–94 neural units were recorded in each session (25 sessions from monkey J, six sessions from monkey L, 11 sessions from monkey N).
source: In each session, 85–94 neural units were recorded (25 sessions from monkey J, six sessions from monkey L, 11 sessions from monkey N).
evidence: This describes the experimental data collection.

claim: The average firing rate of the neural units per session was 50 ± 8, 42 ± 4, and 55 ± 14 spikes/s (mean ± s.d.) for monkeys J, L, and N, respectively.
source: The average firing rate of the neural units per session was 50 ± 8, 42 ± 4, and 55 ± 14 spikes/s (mean ± s.d.) for monkeys J, L, and N, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative description of the experimental data.

claim: Factor analysis was applied to the spike counts recorded during calibration trials to identify the 10D linear subspace (i.e. the 'intrinsic manifold') that captured dominant patterns of co-modulation across neural units.
source: We then applied factor analysis (FA) to the spike counts recorded during these calibration trials to identify the 10D linear subspace (i.e. the 'intrinsic manifold') that captured dominant patterns of co-modulation across neural units (Churchland et al., 2010; Harvey et al., 2012; Sadtler et al., 2014; Athalye et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the data analysis method, supported by citations.

claim: Each animal performed an 8-target center-out task by modulating its M1 activity to control the velocity of a computer cursor.
source: Each animal performed an 8-target center-out task by modulating its M1 activity to control the velocity of a computer cursor.
evidence: This describes the experimental task.

claim: Each session involved two different BCI mappings.
source: Each session involved two different BCI mappings.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: The first mapping was chosen to be intuitive for the animal to use.
source: The first mapping was chosen to be intuitive for the animal to use.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: The second mapping was initially difficult for the animal to use, and the animal was given 400–600 trials to learn to use the second mapping.
source: The second mapping was initially difficult for the animal to use, and the animal was given 400–600 trials to learn to use the second mapping.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Animals learned WMPs better than OMPs.
source: We found that animals learned WMPs better than OMPs.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: 42 WMP sessions were selected and 12 were discarded for analysis.
source: Among the WMP sessions, we further selected those in which the animal learned stable control of the second mapping (42 selected and 12 discarded).
evidence: This describes the data selection process.

claim: When an animal uses a BCI mapping, its internal conception of the BCI mapping can differ from the actual BCI mapping, even during proficient control.
source: When an animal uses a BCI mapping, its internal conception of the BCI mapping can differ from the actual BCI mapping, even during proficient control (Golub et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The animals' angular errors when using the second BCI mapping did not usually return to the original level of error that the animal achieved under the first mapping.
source: Across sessions, the animals' angular errors when using the second BCI mapping did not usually return to the original level of error that the animal achieved under the first mapping (Sadtler et al., 2014) (Figure 5—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data, supported by a citation.

claim: When viewed through the animals' internal models of the BCI mappings, angular errors during the second mapping were more similar to those observed during the first mapping.
source: However, when viewed through the animals' internal models of the BCI mappings, angular errors during the second mapping were more similar to those observed during the first mapping (Figure 5—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis using the internal model estimation.
